utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Bala.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I simply remind you at the outset that the solemn declaration to tell the truth which you took at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply to the evidence today. So we'll continue with the cross-examination by Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Bala. Welcome back. When we were -- when we left off yesterday we were talking about the observations you were making from your home in Pristina. And I think the observations you were making during the day-time were also made with the aid of binoculars. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm getting no interpretation, Your Honour. I think she said "yes" but nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if you could repeat that answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your question was whether I was using binoculars day and night. What I said was, in the night-time I did use the binoculars but in the day-time I also observed things without binoculars.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, in the day-time did you observe things with binoculars? That was my question, actually.

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not during the day-time because I could see well without them. I didn't need the binoculars at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the last paragraph on page 3 of your statement in English describing observations you were making on the 28th of March, your statement contains this sentence: "The Serb forces were shooting at unarmed Albanian civilians, and the Albanian civilians were fleeing." Correct?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. The statement -- in your statement to the OTP says: "The Serb" -- this is your observation. "The Serb forces were shooting at unarmed Albanian civilians, and the Albanian civilians were fleeing."

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th of March, if I may begin a full explanation that way, about 10.00 or 11.00 - I don't know exactly - fighting began in Vranjevc in the Hartica family. And in the afternoon about 2.00 shelling began in the area of Kolovica. The -- that is, the last houses on that hill-side. The fighting in the Hartica family was because the family did not want to abandon its house, refused to do so, and there was shooting and fighting all around the house from where I was, and there was shelling in Kolovica, on the highest part. There one could see tanks near a wood in Kolovica, because the -- and the next day large forces, army forces -- as a result of the bombing at night of the military barracks near Pristina in Lukare, from that time on or from that hill-side there was shelling on -- at Kolovica. And of course we saw -- I also saw and other witnesses saw this, but I saw the shelling from my house and observed people fleeing the area of the shelling, not exactly into the centre, but into areas where there was no shooting and no shelling. So they did leave their houses as a result of shelling in that part of town. I also talked to quite a few people who -- who were still around -- out on the streets, in the side streets, because there's quite a few narrow alley-ways in the area where I live. There were people were traumatised. They didn't know where to go, what to do. They had heard all the shellings, seen all the burning of the houses, seen dead bodies as a result of the shelling. I don't want to go into too many details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That will be enough for the moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I wonder if you remember the question I asked you. Do you remember what I asked you?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me whether I had seen people during the shelling, whether I had seen people having to leave their houses, and so I gave you a chronology of the events of the 28th of March because it was day-time and one could see clearly what was going on in that part of Kolovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, the -- when you listened to my question, is it by a translation into Albanian, is that -- is that what you're getting as my question by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, we're not going down this road for the moment. The English translation doesn't even have a question mark at the end of it because it's actually quite difficult to know what the question was designed to elicit. And I, for one, think the witness's interpretation of your question was perfectly reasonable. I think if you were wanting to ask something specific you should have done so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, you're not looking at my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Am I not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I'm going to show it to you and tell you what it said. My question was, "In the last paragraph on page 3 of your statement in English describing observations you were making on the 28th of March, your statement contains this sentence: 'The Serb forces were shooting at unarmed Albanian civilians and the Albanian civilians were fleeing.' Correct?" That was the question, does it contain that statement? I'll try to be more precise in the future, but that was certainly the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the point of the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The point of the question was to connect her with that part of her statement and have her confirm that that was a true statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've had that confirmation, Mr. Ackerman. That in my book is a statement and it's crying out for the witness to say what she did and then you let her go on uncontrolled until I interrupted because it seemed to me it was going on repeating what we already know. So please exercise greater control over this cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When I interrupted her yesterday you told me not to, so today I can interrupt her. Is that your ruling today, if she doesn't answer the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, that's not the ruling. I'm saying exercise more control. I'm not saying just interrupt when you please. Please don't misinterpret what I am saying, and if you are going to make a -- statements that repeat what a witness has said in her statement with the word "correct" at the end of it, it will be no surprise if someone from a different culture answers the question in the way in which that witness did -- has just done. I'm inviting you to exercise greater control in general over the cross-examination to avoid these misunderstandings. I'm not simply inviting you to interrupt as you please. So please don't misinterpret the instructions I am giving. Now what is it you wanted to say, Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I just would like the record to reflect that the witness actually asked Mr. Ackerman to repeat the question and that then, after that, he also just made a further statement, reading out what she said, without even asking whether this is correct or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that was the bit I was looking at, and I was surprised when he told me the question had "correct" at the end of it, for what that's worth. But there you are, Mr. Ackerman. That just confirms that there was no question ultimately when posed. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll be more careful, Your Honour, and try to do a better job.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you talk about those observations that you were making on that day, on the 28th of March, at one part of your statement you talk about the Serb forces shooting at unarmed people, and then two sentences right before that you talked about an armed family that wouldn't give up their homes and were shooting at the Serb forces. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I said - and I will repeat what I said - that in two parts there were -- there were two different battles in Vranjevc --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what you've already said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Nor, Mr. Ackerman, was your question really necessary. If you're going to point up something that you think is contradictory, which I understand entirely, why can't you then proceed to the question you're going to ask, because we know what the statement says? And all you'll get is another repeat of the whole story.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go now to page 4 of your statement in the first full paragraph, you're talking about the 29th of March, and we have your statement here in quite a lot of detail on this page. You don't need to repeat it because we can all read it. My questions, I hope, will be very simple and easy to answer. You talk about people being removed from their houses, and you were making that observation, you tell us. And in the course of describing that you said: "If there were any persons remaining in the house, they would be either beaten or killed." I want to know if you observed anyone being beaten or killed inside their houses.

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This took place not only in my area, but throughout Kosova --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, the question's very specific. Did you see anyone being beaten or killed inside their houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Being beaten, yes, I did. My neighbour, an 80-year-old man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And how were you able to see inside that person's house?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in his courtyard. The old man was forced to -- was being forced to leave his house. We could hear the old man crying because it was happening close to our houses, and this was an old man who died later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How many people who refused to leave their houses did you observe being killed?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen people -- I saw people that refused to leave their houses. I saw people being pushed at the train station, but I haven't seen anyone who was killed in their own homes. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the answer to the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- after the war I took some statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that's the answer to the question. You're only being asked about what you saw. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You talk in your statement about going to Kosovo Polje. Again, it's in that last paragraph on page 4. And you say: "Just before arriving at the Fushe Kosove railway station, on the left-hand side of the railway track, I saw with my own eyes three or four bodies in different areas between the houses and the railway track." That's what's in your statement and I want to ask you this question: You don't know if these bodies were Albanian or Serb or gypsy or what they were, do you?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we knew that they were the corpses that were close to the houses of Albanians, so these were half-burnt or fully burnt corpses. This was close to the road that leads to Fushe Kosove.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The answer is that you don't know whether they were Serb or Albanian or other, do you? You didn't get off the train and investigate that, did you?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that they were Serb corpses or corpses of other ethnicities. They must have been Albanians because that was their intention, to kill and destroy everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you know, don't you, that a number of Serbs were killed there during the fighting?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. I don't have that information, how many of them were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you know that Serbs were killed, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. It was time of war, so people could get killed on both sides. But in the case of Kosova, the victims were mostly Albanians. During that period of the 78 days of NATO bombing, the Serbs, because of that bombing, tried to take revenge on Albanians and tried to destroy everything Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you got to -- I think it was the Hani i Elezit cement factory where you were told to get off the train and walk along the railroad track, you say you were told to walk in the middle of the track because there were mines on either side, correct?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was this just a single, narrow railroad track, or were there triple, double railroad tracks there, or what?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One single rail line with one track, and I walked along that for 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you were walking along that with a -- a large group of people?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Women, elderly people, handicapped people, children, old people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And were you all walking in single file or were you walking two abreast or three abreast or what? Just kind of describe what that column would look like? Was it a wide column, a narrow column? What was it?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some people walked two or three together. At the time in the evening, I wasn't paying too much attention of how people were walking. The fear was that somebody, because of the terror and the fear and the exhaustion, could step outside the tracks and we would all be blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that was your understanding, that there were mines just outside the tracks, correct?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told. That's what they told us because we didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you say that during that walk down that narrow track with mines on either side, that Serb forces were still standing guard over you and they were separating men from the column and demanding money and identification from them. Now, where were these Serb forces, were they out there in the mine fields?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb forces were at Hani i Elezit where we were told to get off. They were in front of the cement factory. They were not on the Blace side because that was a neutral area. They were in front of the cement factory. I was in the third or the fourth carriage I think. I'm not sure about that. We got off the train, and the Serb forces were around that cement factory. I mean that there were not only three or four or five of them, but there was a long line of them. The whole train was observed and controlled under the control of the force -- of the forces. And they told the males to go to one side and the females to the other side. And they were searching them. Some people were even threatened with the barrels of their guns. It was a very frightening scene. I could see people's IDs being torn up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have answered the question. So let's move on, Mr. Ackerman, to the next one.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to slow down, please, for the interpreters' benefit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, you're also being asked if you could possibly speak a little more slowly to assist the interpreters. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More slowly, yes, I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go back to your job with the OSCE while you were in Pristina. What were your duties in that job? What were you doing?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My duties at the OSCE were those of an assistant for human rights, and the first duty I was given was to monitor the situation in Pristina. That was the basis of my work at the OSCE in Kosova -- or at least for the regional office in Pristina. The other part of my activities, I was also involved in dealing with witnesses for the Recak case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you work as an interpreter at all?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what languages were you interpreting in?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Albanian into English, and from English into Albanian. But from time to time I also interpreted from Serbo-Croatian into English or from Serbo-Croatian into Albanian, in both directions actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I take it to be an English interpreter you had to demonstrate complete fluency in the English language?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a university level, but I would say that I write and speak and understand English quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you told us yesterday that things appearing in your original statement to the OTP might have been there because of a misinterpretation or mistake, that wouldn't be based upon any of your misunderstanding of the language, would it?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an oversight. It might have been someone else's. I don't really know. It was simply a matter of expressions. It's different when you speak in English or speak in your own language. Nothing is done word for word. Things have to be formulated differently, according to the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You are a politically active person, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't politically active until 2001. I was involved in human rights affairs or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was politically active after 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You were a member of I think it's the PDK party or DPK party? You are a member of that party, are you not?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am a member of the Democratic Party of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's the party headed by Hashim Thaqi?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the party headed by Hashim Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact, as you sit here today I think you are a member of the Pristina Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not a member of the parliament of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you ever -- no, not the parliament of Kosovo, the Assembly of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A deputy of the Municipal Assembly until 2005 I was, and in 2005 I withdrew in order to carry on my studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You continue your membership, though, in Mr. Thaqi's party, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am a member of the Democratic Party of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be all my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will have a few additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Bala, my name is Mihajlo Bakrac, attorney-at-law, one of the counsel for General Lazarevic in this case. If I understood properly, you just said that you saw the shelling by the army from Lukare. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shelling was -- took place from a hill between Vranjevc and Kolovica. Behind the hill there was at that time a military barracks of the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Since you mentioned the barracks, is that the barracks in Lukare?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's where the barracks are. Now the Kosovo protection force is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you see what type of armaments they used?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a tank on the top of the hill. It was -- there are no trees on that part of the hill, no vegetation. Simply a bare hill under which the train -- the tunnel goes. It's a hill that you can see from pretty well everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were you aware that in Lukare there were no barracks? There was simply a shelter with supplies there and there was only the group which provided security for the facility and they only had rifles. They didn't have any heavy pieces.

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I know that there were barracks there because I've passed by there, not just once but thousands of times because I have relatives in Lukare and there was a military barracks there and tanks there and trucks and soldiers, everything. And you can see it, it was a -- visible barracks you could see from the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you see from your roof?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I said that the barracks were behind the hill. I could see the tank on the top of the hill, which was firing at -- shelling at Kolovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, did you see that tank during the day or at night-time?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's clear from my statement that I saw it on the day-time, not at night. It was on the afternoon of the 28th of March, I think 2.00 or 3.00 in the afternoon. But it was in -- on that hill near Kolovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And how far away is your terrace from this place where the tank was? What's the distance as the crow flies?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military barracks I think are about a kilometre and a half or two kilometres from Pristina. I don't know how much -- far it would be as the crow flies. The hill is closer because, as I said, the barracks are behind the hill, towards -- in the direction of Lubana [phoen], Vrmice, and other villages, and in the other direction there is a road entering Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I asked you whether you could say what the actual distance was as the crow flies from the terrace to the place where you saw the tank.

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't -- couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that it was at least 500 metres or more than that?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply don't know how far it could be as the crow flies, but we could -- I could see it very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you manage to see any markings on that tank?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I wasn't really paying attention to any insignia or markings on the tank because it was a tank shelling the town and I would imagine that the markings would be very small.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, you were saying that you had binoculars with infra-red rays, night-vision binoculars, and that you used it during the night. Did these binoculars with infra-red light give out some kind of red-coloured signals or do they emit anything that is red?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, I can't follow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that the witness said she had binoculars with infra-red rays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't recollect that either. We've had quite a lot of cross-examination about the binoculars. Is it an area you really need to pursue further?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise but on page 3 of the B/C/S version it says: "I had a pair of infra-red binoculars." Now I'm going to have a look at the English version. In the English version it says "night-vision binoculars." Now I'm asking whether these night-vision binoculars had any red signal or whether it emitted anything red so that one could use it for night-time observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may answer the question now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my statement I said that I had never used binoculars before, and I couldn't tell you what kind of binoculars they were. All I know is that by using them I could see in the distance, but I don't know if they emitted any light. I think there was a -- some sort of green light. But I don't remember what kind of binoculars they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So the binoculars emitted some kind of green light, right?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a greenish light on them, as far as I can remember because it's been seven years now since I had them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bala. But you will agree with me that on page 2 of your statement you said that you were very afraid that the Serbs would get into your house and would do you some harm. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I certainly wasn't expecting anything good from them, not what happened the next day, but -- not because of what happened the next day but because of what was happening throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, my question was: Since you were so afraid and since you didn't want to draw attention in any way, were you not afraid to stand on your terrace at night in a darkened city using binoculars emitting greenish lights? And were you not afraid that you would be noticed by someone three nights in a row?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was not the question that was first put to the witness, that is a new question now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. But the first question was similar to Mr. Ackerman's question of setting the base, so we've moved on. There's nothing wrong with that. Can you answer that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the NATO bombing, I had -- I wasn't afraid at all. I was at home, because during that time I didn't hear any movements, aside from the bombing itself. When the bombing stopped, one could hear shooting, explosions, detonations, movements of trucks, tanks, and vehicles. You could hear cries and shouts. We knew that something terrible was happening somewhere to someone and that we could all be caught up in what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, the question really --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That's not an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Bakrac. The question was whether you didn't think that you might be noticed because of the light that was coming from these binoculars. Now, can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not have that impression at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did they light up in some way that outsiders would be able to notice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was looking straight ahead through the binoculars, I didn't see any -- that I was emitting any light. I was simply looking through the binoculars. I did not have the impression that -- that someone would be seeing -- would be observing me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, you said that you were carefully following what was going on in Vranjevc. You must have noticed on the 27th and 28th of March the KLA attack on the police station in Vranjevc, right?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The police station in Vranjevc is at a much higher position in town, which I couldn't see from where I was. There are houses in that direction. The neighbourhood towards Vranjevc can be seen, but the police station is in a different locality. The Hartica house is quite a -- far away from the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So you just saw part of Vranjevac where the Hartica house is, right?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The portion which was right across from where I was. But on the other side of leaves -- which goes down, which leaves Pristina, I couldn't see because of the hill-side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, did you see any of the members of the Hartica family after the 27th -- or rather, the 28th of March?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any members of the Hartica family.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, a few moments ago you said to my learned friend Mr. Ackerman that the Hartica family was fighting and shooting at the police because they didn't want to leave their house. How come you know that that was the reason why they fought? That's your assumption, right?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not an assumption. I could see the fighting from my terrace, the fighting in Vranjevc with the Hartica family. I could see that they did not want to leave their house, and the people who left that, were leaving their region, with whom I spoke said why -- what the fighting was about. Of course I couldn't see inside the house who was shooting at whom, and the horrors which were taking place there. But people who would come down to my area told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And they were talking to the Hartica family and they knew what the reason for their fight was. Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one actually knew the details because no one could get into that area. The house was surrounded, but that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Bala, I will take you back to the part of your statement where you said that on the 29th of March an officer of the VJ came to your house as well as a gypsy. You explained that this was a traffic policeman, Ivica. Could you please be so kind to describe what this VJ officer looked like. First of all, what kind of uniform did he have?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The officer was wearing a green uniform, a green army uniform, which was easily identifiable. And the traffic policeman, who was our neighbour --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask you about him. I just asked about the officer, and you've given me an answer. Did he have something on his head, this VJ officer?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did he have any kind of insignia on his sleeves?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, on the right side of his jacket, the jacket he was wearing, there was some sort of eagle with red and -- I don't remember the details because I wasn't concentrating on his insignia or on his -- what he was wearing, his boots or his hat. But I did recognise, obviously, that he was a military person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So, Ms. Bala, since you did not notice a single detail except for the colour of the uniform, you're actually just speculating, guessing, that he's a VJ officer, right?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not speculation. It is true he was an officer from the uniform he was wearing. And the way he appeared to us, it was evident that he was a military person of the Yugoslav army. And when we went out on to the same street, we saw other soldiers. He was not alone. There were other soldiers there who -- soldiers, policemen, et cetera, and they were all over the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Bala. Ms. Bala, you said in your statement that when you came to the railway station that there were 30 train cars attached to the engine, and that in the first and the last one there were members of the MUP and of the army. Will you agree with me that 30 train cars have to be at least 600 metres long, right?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we got to the train station, the locomotive was there and so I could see the beginning and the end of the train. There were hundreds, thousands of people waiting there at the train station and we didn't know what was going on. But I did see with my own eyes the locomotive and that they had that many cars. And there are other people who can describe the train. The first part, the beginning of the train where --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No. Ms. Bala, I'm asking you. I'm not asking you about other people's descriptions. I'm asking you. You could see exactly who was in the first train car and who was in the last train car. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they were present there -- I was present there, excuse me. There were hundreds, thousands of people present there. I could see the first part, the locomotive, and the end. It wasn't just a two-car train. There were thousands of people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, do you know Dr. Emin Kabashi?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Emin Kabashi, I know him as a professor who works at the institute of Albanological studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No. I'm just asking you if you know him. Did you see him among those people on that day at the railway station?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where -- you told us where he worked. Could you tell us again where you understand he works?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Emin Kabashi works in the Albanological institute in Kosova. I know him because of the books he has written and various conferences and he's well-known in the whole of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That clarifies the point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, if I were to say to you that Professor Kabashi who testified here did not mention the army at all as being present at the railway station and on the train, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he testified to here, but I know what I saw with my own eyes, and I saw army and policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, will you agree with me a large portion of the civilian population of Albanian ethnic origin remained in Pristina throughout the campaign?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with you because this is not true. That day, on the 29th of --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, Ms. Bala, I'm asking you in general terms, not about that particular day. You have answered and I'm going to move on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry, in my question I said "NATO campaign," so could that please be inserted into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know Adem Demaci, Ms. Bala?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just hold on a second. No, no, hold on just a second. I certainly don't recollect hearing that, but if that was the question then I think it should be posed again to avoid any doubt about what she was answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour, I shall do that. I really did say it. Perhaps the interpreters did not manage to hear me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, is it correct that a number of civilians of Albanian ethnic background stayed in Pristina throughout the NATO campaign?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The citizens of Pristina, for three days in succession left the city, they were forced out of the city. The other part of the inhabitants who lived in Pristina and stayed there during the NATO bombing, these were people who had come from the villages, who were forced out of their villages, and had come to live -- to stay in Pristina as a safe place. These were people coming from the mountains, from the hills, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no, I'm trying to understand this. You say the other part who were people who had come from other villages, are you saying they stayed on in Pristina? Or did they also leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later on, these left as well. But the neighbourhoods were empty, simply empty. I cannot say that the whole city was empty of people, but the majority of the inhabitants of Pristina left the city during those three days. Later people came from the villages, from the mountains, trying to flee the fighting and the war from Llapi and other places. From both sides of Pristina, the population was forced to come to a point which is the Koliq village. They were shelled there and there were hundreds of people who were killed. Then they were sent towards Leskoc. Then on the 1st, 2nd, and the 3rd, the greatest massacres happened in Grashtice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're only at the moment concentrating on how many people stayed in Pristina. That's what I would like to be clear about. Now, are you saying that during these three days there were people who stayed in Pristina or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The overwhelming majority were forced to leave. There were families that remained there, but mostly Turkish, Roma, Bosnian families.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, do you know Adem Demaqi?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I worked with Mr. Demaqi for about seven years in the Council for the Defence of Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have not heard any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There must be a problem with the Serb translation, because the English was translated. Can we have the Serb translation for Mr. Bakrac, please? You got it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then you certainly know that he is one of the political ideologues of the KLA, right?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And do you know that Mr. Adem Demaqi stayed in Pristina throughout the NATO campaign? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I returned from Macedonia, I met Adem Demaqi, and he told me that he had been in Pristina all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: A few moments ago you said that only Bosniaks, Roma, and others stayed behind. Are you trying to say that when the NATO protection force -- or rather the KFOR entered Pristina it was empty. Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not a proper characterisation of the answer, which was, "The overwhelming majority were forced to leave. There were families that remained there, but mostly Turkish, Roma, Bosnian families."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I'll withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, do you know that most Albanian civilians -- or rather, Albanian civilians who stayed behind in Pristina as well as pensioners, that throughout the NATO campaign they were receiving their pensions from the state of Serbia? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, I will just deal with the last part now very briefly. When you went to Macedonia, you said that you went to Ohrid. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived in Macedonia, after some days I contacted people, colleagues, people from my town. And where I was in Negotin, the camp was called Neprosten. There I met my former colleagues from the OSCE mission, and I established my first contacts with them and I joined them and I went to Ohrid in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I understood, Ms. Bala. You spoke about yourself in the first person singular, but what about the rest of your family, where were they?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My whole family was with me the whole time, and we were together in that village, my father; my mother, now deceased; my older brother; the other brother; and the children.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And all along, Mrs. Bala, they were with you on the train, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And no one took their IDs away from them or any belongings of theirs and you were not taken [as interpreted] any of those items either, and you mentioned that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we got off the train, as I said, it was third or fourth car or carriage -- please, let me explain. Is it possible for me to explain myself? You asked me a question and I want to give an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it's necessary at the moment. Let's hear what this is leading to. What's the next question, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour. I just wanted to have this as the last one. I wanted to know whether any belongings were taken from the members of her family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you tell us that that's in her statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I was probably misinterpreted. I meant that it would have been part of her statement had it happened that way. She would have described such experience by others. Had those IDs been taken away, my conclusion would be it would have been part of the statement because that would have been her own experience. Perhaps that was mistranslated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, what is it you want to say about what happened when you got off the train?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we got off the train I was at the beginning of the tracks. It was right there. We got off, and we heard them when they said: Walk straight down the track because it's mined on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you going to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The area is mined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you going to say something about belongings and identification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, could we get to it, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. When the first group started to walk down the tracks, they asked for their IDs and they tore up their IDs. But there were hundreds and thousands of people. So later on they did not ask for the IDs, but the first group, they -- their IDs were tore up and also they were searched, body searches, and I don't know what happened later on because I wasn't there. But I can tell you what I saw while I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't want the witness to describe what she saw but to answer the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Neither you nor any members of your families were taken their identities from? Is that true or not? No belongings were taken?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because we did not have them on us. And when they asked us for our IDs, we told them that we didn't have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Ms. Bala. My name is Branko Lukic, and together with Mr. Ivetic and Ogrizovic, I appear on behalf of Mr. Lukic. You used to work for the OSCE prior to the conflict in Kosovo back in 1990, before the beginning of the NATO campaign. I wanted to pose some questions concerning the work and the findings of the OSCE, and I just wanted to hear from you whether you have any knowledge of that. During your work with the OSCE, did you have any access to the data or any such information that would confirm that the KLA was engaged in killing Albanians who were loyal to the state?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did not have any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said you knew Sandra Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sandra Mitchell was the director of the human rights department while I worked in the regional office of Pristina, and we had another director. She was the director for the whole of the regions of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the data Ms. Mitchell had included the work of all the field offices. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether she included them or not, I don't know. I only know that she was the director of the department. I can only speak here about the Pristina regional office.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 612, in line 11, Ms. Mitchell said, testifying before this Tribunal, that the KLA was killing Albanians who were loyal to the state of Serbia. Would you believe she was telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that. It's not for one witness to express a view on the likelihood that a statement made by another witness was true or not when that witness has none of the information on the basis of which confirmation can be given.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: She said clearly she had no information about the KLA being engaged in killing Albanians loyal to the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Bala, in your statement dated the 30th of June, 2001. In the English page 2, paragraph 3. In the Albanian page 2, paragraph 3. And in the B/C/S, page 2, paragraph 2. You state that the OSCE was preparing that evacuate on the 19th of March. They were getting ready to leave Kosovo and Serbia because an all-low standard of the living of the Albanian community and the violence being instilled for political reasons. Is this still your testimony? Do you still believe this is why the OSCE left Kosovo and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a summary or an introduction to this statement. I didn't want to enter into details about what happened in Kosovo from 1989 up till the moment when OSCE left Kosovo. There was a situation of conflict, war, and the agreement that had been reached with resolution of the United Nations. It was not observed. The conflict was intensified.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would Mr. Lukic please wait for the translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if this cross-examination is designed to elicit some information about ulterior -- other reasons for OSCE leaving, when they left, do you really think that this witness will be in a position to answer these questions, bearing in mind the position she held?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, honestly I do believe because she must be talking with the other members of the OSCE and the reasons why they packed their stuff and left. But if this witness does not want to answer it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no. I just -- it seems to me a pointless exercise and wasting your time, but if that's the line you wish to pursue I can't stop you at the moment. But if it becomes clear that it's inappropriate, then you will be stopped. I'm just trying to assist, but please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask you directly, Ms. Bala. Do you believe that the announced NATO campaign had no influence on the withdrawal of the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that all the diplomatic attempts, the international efforts had been exhausted. There was repression, massacres continued. The agreement was not being implemented, so the OSCE mission could not do anything, so they withdrew.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would Mr. Lukic please wait for the English translation. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic -- Mr. Lukic, you have to wait until the translation is complete. So you'll need to pause before you start questioning the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm trying just to push this questioning forward, Your Honour. We are not moving anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. But if you talk over the -- or if you speak immediately after she has finished speaking, you allow no time for the translation to be completed, and that will not help progress the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Bala, could you please answer. What is your opinion or give me a yes or no, the upcoming or the announced NATO campaign, did it have any influence on the withdrawal of the OSCE mission from Kosovo and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, don't answer that. First of all, Mr. Lukic, you'll have to establish a factual basis for that question, so you'll need to find out what was the witness's knowledge about the upcoming NATO campaign, and then we'll see where we go from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Bala, among the members of the OSCE mission, was there any discussion about a possible beginning of NATO -- of the NATO campaign in Serbia and Kosovo? Were you ever present during such conversations?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My learned friend Mr. Ackerman attempted to clarify a part of your statement dealing with -- it is in English on page 2, paragraph 4; in Albanian, page 2, the last paragraph; and in B/C/S, page 2, paragraph 3. And there you mention that the Albanian civilians told you that they were sending their families away or out of Pristina out of fear.

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained, clarified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Wait until a question is asked, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman compared that to another statement of yours dated the 16th of August, 2006, and it's item seven or paragraph 7. I wanted to ask you this: Concerning the notes of the interview that were given by the OTP, and the interview was conducted on the 14th of April, 1999, and in -- it's item 8 of that statement where you also state the following: "The local population was getting ready for a Serb invasion, and some sent their families out of Pristina." How do you explain this, that for the second time we find this in your statement and yet you claim it not to be true?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained yesterday this paragraph when Mr. Ackerman asked me, and I frankly don't know what else can I explain in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In what language was the interview conducted on the 14th of April, 1999, Ms. Bala?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it your explanation that you made the same mistake you did at another occasion when you spoke English, or is there something else that may clarify this situation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I don't think this is a proper question because if any mistake it was made, it was made by the investigator who took down these notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's your assertion, Ms. Moeller. What we're at the moment doing is exploring evidence, and the question relates to a different document, although the same point, and there's nothing wrong with asking the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It's not established that this was ever read back to the witness or that she ever saw these interview notes even.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I understand that, but I see nothing wrong with the question. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already said that I gave this explanation yesterday and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I interrupt? Who was it you spoke to in April 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I can't remember who it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We know from your statement in June 2001 you spoke then to a man called Stephen Leach. Was it a different person you spoke to in April 1999 or could it have been the same person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be honest, I can't remember. It's been a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you'll understand the point that's being made by Mr. Lukic. If it was two different people you spoke to and they both reflected your account in the same way, then it is difficult to blame the investigators rather than accept responsibility yourself. I think that's the point that's being put to you, although perhaps not as clearly as that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Honourable Judge. I'm not trying to blame anyone about this, but the way -- when I explain myself in English and the way I explain myself in Albanian, those are different and maybe that brought up this misunderstanding. What I said and what I am saying now is that these people were uncertain about the future. They didn't know what to do with their families. They did not say that they were sending their families to Albania or somewhere outside Kosovo. Their idea was to take their families somewhere safe, and this is -- was the general idea among the whole of the -- among all the people I was speaking with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic, I think that document should be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We just intended to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it in the system and does it have a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it, if the Prosecutor put it in the system. I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think the Prosecution have. It's a matter for you. You're relying on this document now. So it has to get into the system somehow. So it will be -- it will be the next number after the last number of your exhibits at the moment, so it will be 6D, whatever your last one is plus 1. Can you give me that number?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Should be 68, 6D68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. And it's for you now to introduce it into the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we just received this yesterday. We printed it last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's in your hands to do that forthwith. Now, let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that the electricity was cut off in Pristina on occasion. This is in English page 2, paragraph 5; in the B/C/S and the Albanian --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not manage to catch the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English, page 2, paragraph 5; in the Albanian, page 3, paragraph 1; in the B/C/S, page 2, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was electricity cut off only to the Albanian population of Pristina or to the entire population of Pristina?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the NATO bombing started, at that moment the electricity was cut off. And after the air attacks stopped, then electricity would come back on. I would say that the electricity was cut off in the whole of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also mentioned check-points. In paragraph 1, page 2 in the English; in Albanian, paragraph 2, page 3; and B/C/S, page 2, the last paragraph. There you state that check-points were surrounded by barbed wire. Can you still observe similar check-points today manned by KFOR?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such check-points in various parts of Kosova did exist, used to exist, but these checkpoints did not -- do not exist anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did KFOR check-points exist in the past and do they still exist in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there are check-points of the security and police forces, but these check-points are not the same as they used to be with the barbed wire. They are just normal check-points. On one side there is the KFOR and then on the other side it's the Kosova police. It's something that is very normal, but these are not inside the towns. They are outside the towns where they carry out their own daily duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My learned friend Mr. Bakrac asked you today at page 18, line 2, whether you saw the attack at the police station in Vranjevc. You said: No, because you weren't able to see that part of Vranjevc. Yesterday at page 2.152, line 21, you said you could see all of Vranjevc. So could you see all of Vranjevac or not?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main hill of Vranjevc I can see. Even today I can see it from my house, but then the outside, the slope, that goes down - and it's the road that leaves Pristina - I cannot see that, but the main hill-side I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do you have many more questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not too many, Your Honour, but if it would be an appropriate time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily. Mr. Fila, do you have questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, yes, Your Honour. And I will have an objection; therefore, I will need to lay a foundation for that. But I will have this little questions -- of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now and resume at five past or just after five past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I reduced my questions as much as possible, and I hope I will finish soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Bala, most of us have never been to Pristina, and that is the reason why we are asking these questions about the geography of your town as well. Again, I have to go back to page 36, line 19, so that you could tell me where the police station is at Vranjevac.

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exact street I don't know, but there is still a police station there and -- as there was at the time. It's when you leave -- are leaving Pristina, in that part of town, at the edge. It's not in the centre of Vranjevc, but it's right at the end of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why did you not see police station when it was attacked? Because it's on the other side of the hill or because there is something marring the view?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the police station when it was being attacked, as I said. But I don't know what happened, how or when. I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the question is: Why couldn't you see it? Again -- I think you've been asked it already, but you're being asked again. What was obstructing your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's -- as I said, it's a part of town that's going downhill. It's not the uphill part which we could see from the centre of town, from my part. It was behind all the houses, on a slope going down, and I couldn't see it from where I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you, because on page 18, line 5, and I'm going to read it so I don't misinterpret it. When you say why you did not see the attack on the police station you say: [In English] "The police station in Vranjevac is at a much higher position in town. There are houses in that direction." [Interpretation] So could you not see it because of what you said on page 18 or because of the reasons that you mentioned now in your last answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, read the next answer on page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "There are houses in the direction. The neighbourhood towards Vranjevac can be seen, but the police station is in a different locality."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then read the next answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "So you just saw part of Vranjevac where the house was, right?" And your answer was: "The portion which was right across from where I was. But on the other side of leaves -- which goes down, which leaves Pristina. I couldn't see because of the hill-side." I apologise, Your Honour, I only read it partially. I apologise, and I withdraw this question. Can I move on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Bala, do you know that on the 26th of March in Dragodan a policeman was killed in a terrorist attack?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said -- told you what I saw on the 26th of March, and that was the burning of a house. I don't know about this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You're talking about Vranjevac. In the English version page 3, paragraph 5; Albanian, page 3 -- or rather, page 4 of the Albanian version, paragraph 2; and the B/C/S version, paragraph 3 -- paragraph 5 on page 3. You talk about fighting in Vranjevac and you say that the Hartica family put up a resistance for two hours and then the Serbs shelled their houses. Do you know how many people took part in this armed resistance?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you because I wasn't on the site, but I do know that the family, the Hartica family, was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the logistics base of the KLA was at Vranjevac, one of the logistics bases of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that there were the -- that there were armed forces of the police and the army there in Vranjevc, but I don't know of any forces of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just like to ask you something else now, about the moment when you were at the railway station. And you say that civilians were shouting at you, that they were saying: What are you waiting for? Kill them. Don't let them go away to Albania. Did these civilians try to attack you physically?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the street, in the centre of town, of Pristina, which leads from the committee building downwards toward the police -- towards the train station, there were, aside from policemen and soldiers and other uniformed individuals and armed civilians who I'd never seen before, there was cursing, shouting from -- also from civilians in apartment buildings. They were throwing bottles at us, they were playing loud music. They were saying things like: What are you waiting for? What are you waiting for? Kill them, kill them. I could hear them because I understand -- I understand Serbian quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But no one attacked you, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what do you think throwing bottles is, Mr. Lukic? I mean, the question's been answered. Does it need any further exploration?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may pose just another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did anyone protect you from these civilians?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one at all. The objects which were being thrown at us from the apartment buildings, no one even tried to protect us from them or to say anything to those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that you will agree with me that it's very hard to protect someone from something that was thrown from a building. Is it not a fact that these civilians who were at the same level where you were and who were threatening you did not actually attack you, they did not manage to attack you?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their psychological violence, physical violence. If things are being thrown at you from upper floors of buildings, that is violence, and it certainly -- it certainly was no coincidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bala. Those are all the questions I had for you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Bala, my name is Toma Fila, and together with my colleague, Mr. Petrovic, I am Defence counsel for Nikola Sainovic. I want to ask you something that Mr. Ackerman first started dealing with. He pointed out to you that at the end of your statement, when you made this witness acknowledgement, you signed the statement saying that the statement had been read out to you in the Albanian language. And also he indicated to you that in addition to your own signature on the right-hand side on the other side - right? - that on the left-hand side Mr. Leach signed the same acknowledgement confirming that that is what it was. Look at the last page if it's not clear to you. Do you know who translated this statement to you into Albanian so that it could be read out to you?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just find the last page and you'll see it straight away.

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. The name of the translator, as you can read yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I can't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can't see a name for a translator, nor does it say in the statement that there was a translator present.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, sorry, you mean the first part?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your statement dated the 30th of June, 2001, this one single statement. You haven't got another statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm getting a signal from the Prosecution bench that that's wrong, but I can't at the moment see where there's a reference to the translator.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I think the witness hasn't found the right page yet, Your Honour, and it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Nor have I.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, I understand Mr. Fila to talk about the last page of her first statement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but there's no reference there to a person who may be said to be an interpreter, is there?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Not that I would see it, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. So that's his point.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, I did not say that such a person was present. I never said that. That's what the witness said. So you work it out with the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's the witness who has said that there was a translator who read it to her, and he's asking what the translator was. That seems a perfectly reasonable question to me. So can you help us who translated this statement into Albanian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I might explain. I believe we are talking about the final declaration which I signed. There seems to be a very simple explanation to the confusion. I can see here my signature -- well, the year 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I've found the right page. So I was looking at the wrong side of the page. The Tribunal, their office in Pristina, all international staff there have interpreters with them, not only with me -- for me, but for all other witnesses who give statements, either in Albanian or in English. The procedure is --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are just wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why do you say that, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am trying to ask a very simple question. Let's not waste any time. On that page that she finally found, on the right-hand side she signed it, on the left-hand side Mr. Leach signed it. They both signed it and they both signed that this statement had been read out to her in the Albanian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My question is: Does she know who it was who read it to her in the Albanian language. I don't want to listen to this entire tirade. Does she know or doesn't she?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember the name of the interpreter because the interpreters were constantly changing there every six months, so I don't remember the exact name. I couldn't tell you at the moment. .

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. But you remember that the statement was translated for you?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you look at the first page, if you look at page 1 now. Please go back to page 1 now. You will see that during the interview it is only the investigator who is present and Ms. Bala. Again, there is no interpreter or translator there. So who was it who could have translated this for her if there was no one present? The statement was given in English. Ms. Bala, you're inventing all of this.

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all, sir, Mr. Toma Fila, I'm certainly not inventing all of this. I know what statements I gave, and I know when an interpreter was there. There was a translator there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, I'm not going into the merits of your statement. I'm not asking all of this in order to insult you. You are trying to save yourself from something that you don't have to save yourself from. Quite simply, there were no interpreters there and you and Mr. Leach signed something that never happened. That is a simple solution and that is the way it certainly was.

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're trying to say here. In the procedures of The Hague Tribunal there are formalities, as you can see here. I can't understand it, but there was an interpreter there --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, nobody read the statement to you because everything was being carried out in English. Could you please explain to me why would somebody translate this statement to you that -- into Albanian since you were conducting the interview in English anyway? What point would be made that way? Now you're trying to prove something that doesn't make any sense at all. And actually, my objection is against --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's have the -- let's have a simple question. You -- you were the one criticising the witness for giving us a tirade, I think was the word you used.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, your own -- to ask this question is more of a speech than a question. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The last point was argumentative, and I think the witness already now twice answered the question whether an interpreter was there or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Fila makes the further point which he seeks from Ms. Bala which is that it seems pointless having this translated into Albanian when you understand your English so well and the interview was conducted in English. And he's asking you to take that into account and explain why on earth anyone would translate it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the procedures of The Hague Tribunal, and they know what to do. All statements have to be translated into Albanian, and it wasn't my decision. These are the procedures, the regulations, of the Tribunal. The language I gave my statement in, it is true that I spoke Albanian, but I don't remember how it was on that day. When they brought me the paper copy, in which language it was, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, you don't remember whether it was in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you say that again, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
