utterances.text: You can't remember whether the statement was written in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement I gave was written directly in English by the person who took the statement from me, and later it was translated into Albanian to ensure the exactness of the contents and in accordance with the regulations of the Tribunal that such statements have to be translated into Albanian or into B/C/S. Such are the regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not ask about what happened later. I'm talking about that day. She and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Continue with your questions, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, on that day we see from your statement that you and Mr. Leach were the only persons present and that no one else was present during the course of your interview and you signed that. There was no interpreter there, there was no translator there because you were conducting the interview in English. That is what you signed on page 1, and you signed that there was no one else there, except for the two of you. Please look at page 1.

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I have to go back to the year 2001, I have to explain and I can explain very clearly what happened and very briefly. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question is more specific. The question is: Why did you sign this first page to the effect that there were only two persons present if there was a third person present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third person was not involved in the statement taking, but later the statement was translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It says here that no other person was present. It says here on page 1: Names of all persons present during interview. Only those two persons: She and Mr. Leach. So one of the two signatures is wrong. There either was a third person or there was not a third person there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's been answered, Mr. Fila. She's told you there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. I'm not going to go into this any further. The question -- why I put this question is not to insult you, Madam, but because when we are given such statements --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you, Your Honour, insist that the trial should proceed speedily, whoever wanted to see this statement had to see straight away that it is senseless that someone would translate to her all of this into Albanian when she was conducting the interview in English. And you allowed my learned friend Mr. Ackerman and me to waste half an hour of our precious time to prove something that anyone can see. So I do apologise to you, therefore, for being on my feet to put these questions, but I've kept silent so many times. For example, when I saw translations when they say about Prascevic that he was doing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I'm making no complaint about what you're doing, you're exploring this, and you're allowed to as you require. But you don't need to ask any questions more than once when you've got the answer. That's all I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. But I am so sorry that I wasted all this time in order to prove something that was so evident. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic or Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't intend to help us on this point?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: On the point with the statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Most of these statements do demonstrate that -- do include the name of an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, but I don't know how the witness could actually help with that. I think -- but I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no, I just thought you might have been able to, but if you don't know the situation for sure, then there's nothing you can do to help. I'm just slightly surprised that there's nothing on the document to indicate who was the person who was involved in the interpretation. Do you not usually record that in some way?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: We do, Your Honours, in the more recent statements, but it depends on the individual interpreter who actually types those statements, on whether he includes all persons present or not and how decent a statement is or not. But I would actually -- on this occasion I would like to put one question to the witness maybe to clarify one aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, I understand that you said when the actual interview was taken it was only you and Mr. Leach present. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain it. There was also a translator with Mr. Leach, but because I gave my statement in English there was no need for this translator to translate -- to interpret everything to -- back to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I guess --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that's probably why.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. So the interpreter only became active once Mr. Leach had typed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's have no leading questions in re-examination. If you're going to re-examine properly at this point, then do it with entirely open questions, because it's not of any use to us at this stage to have leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But I would submit that it would be of importance to us knowing how you followed this procedure of taking down a statement. And if you're not in a position today to answer this question, may I, with permission of my Lord Bonomy, request you to kindly ascertain and let us know so that things are clarified, because this is a procedure you follow. And a witness is not supposed to know what procedure you follow so that these confusions do not take place later.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. No, I'm afraid I disagree with Judge Chowhan on this, so we'll need to have a discussion about it. Just give us a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, we're confining our attention at the moment to the statement that you gave on the 30th of June, 2001, in which you were interviewed by Stephen Leach. Now, while he was interviewing you, who was present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Aside from me, there was Stephen Leach, and he asked me in which language I would like to give my statement, in English or in Albanian. I told Mr. Leach that I spoke and read English and that I would give my statement in English. So there was no need for it to be interpreted into Albanian on the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that wasn't my question, so I'll ask you the question again. While Stephen Leach was interviewing you, who was present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His translator was present during the interview, but in fact during the statement in English that I gave, she did not intervene because there was no need for an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, throughout the period, from the time the interview began until you signed the last page, the witness acknowledgement, what did the interpreter do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She listened to our conversation, but she did not interpret into Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'll ask you that question also again, and again I'll be grateful if you'll listen to the question. Throughout the period, from the time the interview began until you signed the last page, the witness acknowledgement - and you've read that, you know what it says - throughout that whole period I want you to tell me what the interpreter did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was a very small room with a computer in it and a telephone and other equipment, and during the whole time she listened to our conversation. She was present with us in the room. She wasn't outside. She was present. But, as I said, I asked her -- I told her there was no need to interpret into Albanian because I understand English and I can give my statement in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Bala, why then did you sign a statement which says it was read over to you in the Albanian language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I signed the page as part of the procedure and didn't read it over, I guess, word for word. I just looked at it in general, that it was a witness acknowledgement, which said that my statement was true to the best of my knowledge and didn't look at that part of the acknowledgement. I simply didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, Mr. Fila, have you any more questions arising from that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only one. If you look closely at today's transcript, 15 or 20 minutes ago, she said that the interpreter indeed interpreted the statement into Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... do you have any more questions to ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my question: What the difference was, which of the two was correct, the one she said 15 minutes ago or what she is saying now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You really want to ask that question, do you? Okay, well, let's have the answer to that. You told us 15 or 20 minutes ago, says Mr. Fila, that the interpreter interpreted the statement into Albanian, and you certainly have said that in your evidence. And now you're saying that that didn't happen, that you simply were signing an acknowledgement that the statement was true. Now, which of these accounts, which are not consistent, is accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was a long period of time. The translated version of my statement, translated into Albanian, was given to me the next day to see whether the contents were accurate. The interpreter had been in the office with me all the time, but as I said I asked her not to interpret into Albanian during the interview because I know English. As I said, the written translation of the document, not the oral version, it wasn't the oral version which was interpreted but the written version which was given to me in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, Ms. Moeller, that sounds like a document none of us has seen -- sorry, did you have another question, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say what you had just said, we want to see those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That sounds like a document none of us has seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: There is an Albanian version of her statement and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That was compiled the day after the statement was taken?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I would have to check the date, Your Honours. I'm just told by my case manager it's part of the 92 bis package, but we don't have the date the statement was translated available right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that is something that can be confirmed to us, can it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, we will check that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Do you have any other questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, I have a couple of questions and I request you to kindly give me your answers to clarify certain things which I thought were necessary. Now, at the Dragodan hill and at Kodra, you were informed of what happened mostly. Did you witness anything yourself or was it only on the statement of the Hartica family or the -- Ms. Hasbia [phoen] that you were informed and that knowledge you were imparting here before us?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I saw in Dragodan is mentioned in my statement, that is the burning of the house and the -- I heard the explosions, et cetera. And in the statement I said that there was fighting in Vranjevc at the house of the Hartica family. And later when the population was expelled from that area or the areas where we lived, I spoke to the inhabitants, not in great detail, but I heard what had happened in general because they were closer to the incident than I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: You said: A woman by the name of Hasbia Krasniqi was one of those who described to me what happened. The shooting and exploding continued throughout the night. Could you kindly tell us what you mean by this, what you mean really was happening?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true. I spoke to Hasbia Krasniqi who came from part of Kolovica. Her house was quite close to the other houses that were shelled, and she informed me that quite a few people had been killed and many had been wounded and there was substantial damage in the houses. And during the whole time from 2.00 in the afternoon until the evening, the -- the incident -- the attack continued on that -- in part of Kolovica. But the shelling was not only against Kolovica but in other areas of town, too. But I couldn't tell exactly which areas were being attacked. The next day, when I talked to people from those areas, I heard that the shelling was coming from behind the area of Taslixhe, the area between Taslixhe and Kolovica. The houses had been under fire from 6.00 in the evening, but -- I can't remember the exact name of the neighbourhood, but later I did get information from witnesses who had been there, and they said that there were victims, both killed and wounded, because there had been snipers there and houses had been burnt. It was on the edges of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Could you be a bit more specific about Kodra. What did you really see there?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kodra is the area in general, the hill-side in general, and I could see the houses on the upper part of the hill-side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: You mentioned about the gypsies also joining, allegedly, with others and forcing you to do certain things. Now, who were these gypsies, and had they then by that time turned towards your opposite side or were they against yourself even before?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Roma or gypsies, as I said in my statement, were mobilised. They had put on police uniforms, but we could see that they were not normal policemen, you know, from the way they wore their hair, and the way they wore the uniform and the shirt, they just put a police jacket over their normal shirt and had something about police written on it. Were wearing jeans, for instance. So we could see that they had been mobilised, but at the same time we could see that they were working with the Yugoslav police and army, and later, I described this, that they had -- were wearing long hair and had paint on their faces, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: At the Dragodan hill you boarded the train. Am I right? Along with others. Did you -- were you carrying anything with you or were you empty-handed? And whatever you were carrying, was that snatched? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All we had with us was milk for the two children because we didn't have time to take anything else with us. There were over a hundred people with us from different areas of Pristina that were staying in my house at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm thankful for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bala. That completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, do I rightly --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in order to conclude with the topic I raised, I would kindly ask the Chamber to put an obligation on the OTP to tell us who wrote that, what the date is of the translation we received, which is ERN 03078246. This is the translation of the statement into Albanian, and we want to know when it was translated and by whom so as to be able to corroborate whether indeed it was translated the next day, as the witness put it, although I sincerely doubt that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I expect we shall get that information in light of what Ms. Moeller told us. So you can draw it to my attention if you don't within a reasonable time receive the information you're looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Moeller, do I rightly see that the next witness is K-63?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that arrangements need to be made in the court for that witness to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That's what we have been told by the technical people that they would be need 20 minutes to set up the voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The practice seems to have evolved as a routine now of you feeling obliged to ask questions of witnesses from whom we have a perfectly clear statement. Are you intending to do that in respect of this witness also?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, I was intending to put a couple of questions to him, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A couple is a very loose term.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I was anticipating not more than 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's more than a couple of questions. I think I ought to alert you to the fact that the Tribunal -- the Chamber will not find exploration of events prior to 1998 in live testimony at the stage of evidence in chief to be a useful exercise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I was not intending to lead any evidence in this regard with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I think what we'll do is we'll take our half-hour break now, which means that we'll resume at 5.30, but we'll sit through from 5.30 to 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we break, could I maybe get an indication, I know it's an early one, but we have the witness after the next witness also waiting here, and I think probably could be released for the day, but could we maybe inquire with the Defence about their intentions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, can you assist on that? That would mean: Is the cross-examination likely to be less than half an hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: At this point, I can't assist you on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Is any counsel clear in his mind that there will be significant cross-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, based upon the number of topics that I have prepared for questioning, I anticipate my cross will last from about 30 to 40 minutes. I can obviously try and cut it down if that assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well, the next witness may be excused in that event.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Good afternoon. Can you hear what I am saying in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Now, we have before us a statement of your evidence, so we know a great deal already about what you have to say. The purpose of this afternoon is to enable counsel to ask any additional questions they wish to ask. And because we already have so much information, it's very important that you do your best to restrict your answer to the particular point that is raised in the question that's asked of you. The first person to ask questions then will be on behalf of the Prosecution, Ms. Moeller. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. As --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: As a first point, I would like to remind you that you should not mention your name or the name of your wife or the country you are currently residing in, to keep your identity and privacy protected.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could the usher please show the witness a sheet for identification purposes. This is Exhibit P2266, and I ask the court officer not to publish it because we will tender it under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Witness, is that your correct name on this sheet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sorry. Can this sheet be shown to the Bench, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Witness, you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on 27 and 28 May 2003. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And on 21st August, 2006, you -- you signed a certification here in The Hague that this is your evidence in the case and that your statement is true and correct, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can the usher show the statement to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you have a look at the statement, Witness, and say whether this was the statement we were talking about, and this is the declaration that you signed here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would like to tender this statement under seal. It's Exhibit Number P2249.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, both these exhibits, 2266 and 2249 will be held under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Witness, are you married?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could the usher please show another sheet to the witness. Thank you. This is Exhibit Number 2265, and we ask the usher not to publish that. And we also tender this under seal, if the witness confirms.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Is that the name of your wife on this sheet, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: We tender this under seal, Your Honours, 2265.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That also will be held under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we bring up Exhibit P13 on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: In the meantime, Witness, where were you living in 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: In Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like the witness to mark two locations where he lived and where his business was, and I would like to go into private session for that, to exclude any possibility that that could identify him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have private session for this part of the evidence, to ensure protection of the identity of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And please remove the map from the screen first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: In paragraph 16 of your statement, you mention a police officer nicknamed Rambo seizing your license in January 1999, and you mention him on other occasions throughout your statement. How did you know he was a police officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I knew that he was a police officer because he had markings on his chest, insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: What kind of insignia were these?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: As far as I know, he had two lines on both sides. The colour was about reddish, a reddish colour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what was the colour of the uniform, if he wore any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: It was the police uniform, dark green and like a wooden colour I would say, some kind of brown colour, I mean the uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Did it have any pattern?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: No, just the badge and the markings, the insignia on both sides of his chest. It was camouflage. I would call it camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: In paragraph 7 of the statement you also referred to this man nicknamed Rambo. You say that: "He told us he was a sector supervisor." Did he tell that to you personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 19 of the statement you are talking about the police coming to your business and ordering food without paying. How did this police, Serb police, look as you described them, Serb police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: The Serb policeman was about 1 metre, 85 centimetres tall, pale complexion, white face. His hair was short cut. His -- the colour of his hair was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sorry, can I interrupt you there. I think we misunderstood each other. I was not asking about a specific policeman, about Rambo, anymore, I was asking about your statement that Serb police came to your shop and demanded to be given food without paying, generally Serb police as you state in paragraph 19 of your statement. Can you describe how you knew they were Serb police. What did they wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, I don't think they were regular policemen. They were paramilitaries with camouflage uniforms and there were seven of them at the time or ten of them at the time. They ordered food, and they did not pay for it. And I was afraid to ask them to pay, although sometimes I did ask them to pay and they just didn't pay me. They just left with the food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller, this is a war crimes trial, not a trial about who stole the pies. We really need to get some perspective into our live testimony here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think these aspects are actually crucial and go to the heart of the case because it's about identification of the forces who were in the city in 1999 and who he observed on several occasions and who he constantly called Serb police. I'm just trying to identify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Show me how the forces in paragraph 19 are related in the statement to those who are said to have committed the crimes that we are concerned about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, he refers to the same term "police" with regard to the events that he then describes on the day he was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I know that, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That's one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How does the evidence we've just heard, which is unspecific to time, help us work out who are the Serb police forces referred to later in the statement? I find it very difficult to see that this is really helpful to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: On 1st April 1999, you referred to that in your statement that you were called to come home. What were you told when you arrived at home, at your apartment, on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: It was midday, about 12.30. I was in my shop working, and the phone rang. And there was this lady who was a neighbour of ours, and she told me: Come home immediately. I told her: I have work to do here at the shop. And she said: You have to come home immediately. So I went there. I drove home. I went inside the flat, and I saw my wife tearing at her face, covering her face with her hands. And I asked that lady: What has happened? What happened here? And she told me: Your wife was raped by three paramilitaries and they left. And then I sat down with my wife, trying to calm her down, but it was impossible to calm her down. This is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Did your wife describe the men to you who raped her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: At that moment she said there were three paramilitaries with -- wearing masks, black masks, camouflage uniforms. And at that moment, in fact, she wasn't sure what the uniform -- what the uniforms were like, just that they had masks on their faces.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Let's move on to 3 April 1999. This is paragraph 33 of the statement. You said that you were expelled that day from your flat. How many Serbs were living in your neighbourhood? And don't mention the neighbourhood now, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: In our neighbourhood there were about 60 per cent Serbs. They did not stay there all the time. Some of them went away, others came, but I would say 60 per cent. But when they came to expel us, the police came and told us to leave our homes. We didn't know where to go, but we just started to leave our homes. When we left our homes, we saw groups of people going down-town, and the groups were joining each other. People were crying, the children were crying, the elderly were crying, the women were crying. So we joined one of those groups and walked with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the Serb people living in your neighbourhood, were they expelled that day, too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: No, they were not expelled. I only remember one woman, a Serb woman, living on the third or the fourth floor. She came out and said: Why are you expelling these people? These people are innocent. And one paramilitary or a policeman, I can't remember what he was, told her: Go inside or otherwise I will kill you. I will kill you instead of killing these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, moving on to the time when you arrived at Pristina train station, this is paragraph 35 of the statement, were there any Serbs waiting to get on the trains out of Pristina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: No. The Serbs were not leaving Pristina; it was only Albanians. We went down-town. When we arrived close to the centre, there were policemen on both side, on the left and on the right. They were shouting, shouting abuse, and they were saying: You have to leave this place. And as I told you, the groups joined each other, got together, and went towards the railway station. Before getting to the railway station, a police car that had stopped there -- there were two policemen on the side of the road that was -- that were beating a young man in the car. And there were two young women.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's stop here. The trains took you to the Macedonian border, as you state in paragraph 38 of your statement. In your statement you say: "The Yugoslavian military was there." What do you mean by "Yugoslavian military"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: The Yugoslavian military were in the border between Kosovo and Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what is the Yugoslavian military? How did they look? Which uniforms did they wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: The Yugoslav army previously had a kind of uniform that we called SNB, while after the 1990s the uniforms changed, the military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: How did they look in 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: In 1999, I'm not very good with colours. I can distinguish green and brown. I knew that they had camouflage uniforms, but I think the army uniform was brown and green but a little lighter in colour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, the last three questions. The first one is: Did you leave Kosovo because you were afraid of NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: No. I left Kosova because the paramilitaries and the Serbian police forced us to go to another country, displaced us from Kosovo. I didn't want to leave Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how is the state of health of your wife today, after those rapes happened to her seven years ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I don't know how to describe my pain and my wife's pain. She -- it is very difficult to describe it in words because one has one life only, and to be faced with such a situation is very difficult. It is difficult for me, but it is much more difficult for her. She is ill. She has flashbacks. She will never forget what happened that day. Her health is very poor. Her nervous system has broken down. From 65 kilogrammes that she weighed in Kosova, now she weighs 43 kilogrammes. That shows you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how is the living situation for you and your wife today in the country you are living in - and please don't mention this country - and -- seven years after you were expelled from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Our living conditions are good. Financially and morally, these are very good conditions. The people there understand us very well. We try to lead a normal life, a good life.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes my questions. I would only have one more request, namely that the IC exhibits are also put under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Moeller. Mr. Sabbah, please attend to that. These will be held under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Exhibits IC18 and IC19 will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: IC 18 and 19?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, first will be counsel for General Lukic, and thereafter will we'll follow the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir. My name is Dan Ivetic, and I am one of the attorneys representing Sreten Lukic, and I'm joined by colleague Mr. Ozren Ogrizovic and Mr. Branko Lukic, who is not with us in the courtroom at present. We are going to have to ask you some questions about your knowledge of events in 1998 and 1999 in Kosovo-Metohija relating to the statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor. Now, first of all, the written statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor dated the 27th and the 28th of May, 2003, that statement was read back to you verbatim in the Albanian language before you signed it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask you then, sir, did you in fact sign the statement dated the 27th and 28th of May, 2003?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes, I signed it there. Where I gave the statement, there is the place where I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, at the time that you signed it, was the statement read back to you in the Albanian language so that you could understand it before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Are you talking about 2003?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I'm talking about 2003, specifically the 28th of May, 2003.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes, on the 28th of May, 19 -- sorry, 2003, I signed the statement and I handed it in, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I need to know whether in fact the statement was read back to you in Albanian, a language you understand, prior to you signing the statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Of course it was read to me -- it was read back to me. Before I signed it, it was read to me and the statement was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And that's why you signed it, because you affirmed that everything that was read back to you from the statement in Albanian accurately reflected what you had told the interviewer. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes. The words I said were true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- strike that. Now, I want to ask you a couple of questions regarding that statement that you signed in 2003 for the Office of the Prosecutor. Now, first of all, at paragraphs 6 and 7 of that statement you talk about certain raids that were undertaken by persons you describe as police. Could you please tell me, while conducting these activities what type of uniforms did these police wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: The police had the same uniform that I mentioned earlier. As I said, I can distinguish basic colours, but not the colours in detail. So they had the same kind of uniform, the same kind of colour, as I mentioned earlier. They came and raided the places, the shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just want to make something -- make sure that the transcript is accurate and the translation is accurate. Are you telling us that you have difficulty in distinguishing colours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I can distinguish them, but -- yeah, I can say that -- you could say that. I cannot distinguish them very well. The basic colours like green, white, black, and red, and brown, I can distinguish them. But colours in between, it's difficult for me to distinguish them, light brown, dark brown, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, does it mean that you are colour-blind for some colours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: It means that sometimes the eyes do not recognise certain colours, and when that happens people are called as colour-blind. But what you are stating is as if you were partially colour-blind and not fully. I just wanted you to kindly answer that because it would get cleared.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already said that white, red, black, and green, I can distinguish these colours very well. But then when it's half blue or dark blue or light blue, things like that I cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll try and proceed and hopefully get some clarity with respect to this testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could remain for a few moments on this event from 1996 and 1997 that is set forth in paragraphs 6 and 7, can you tell us what type of -- strike that. What type of pattern did the persons you have labelled as police have on their uniforms at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I said that those policemen had dark green uniforms together with some brown, maybe light brown, but it was camouflage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In -- you're being asked about 1996 and 1997 at the moment. In 1999, were the uniforms the same or different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The uniforms changed all the time. I would say they changed the uniforms regularly. It was never the same uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And in saying that, are you referring to the regular police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not the regular police, the others, the paramilitaries that came because the police, the regular police, had their uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what colour was their uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were similar colours, but I can -- I could distinguish them because of the badges and they had belts and they had these markings on the left or the right of their chests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking you these questions is that in your statement when you're talking about the 24th of March, 1999, you describe the police as wearing blue camouflage. Now, that sounds different from what you've been describing so far. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was talking about the normal police, but the others who expelled us from our houses, they had different uniforms, not like the regular police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the description I've just given you was relating to the 24th of March, the first day of the bombing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And on that occasion you described all able-bodied Serb civilians as having been put into the police. They were wearing police uniforms and carrying guns. They wore mainly the blue camouflage of the police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, blue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, are these regular police officers or are these paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's what the reservists and the paramilitary had, but the police themselves had blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did not have blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm more confused now than I was when we started, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's why I'm handing it back to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll try and do my best to clear it up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you lived and worked in Pristina for a considerable period of time. What colour uniforms did you notice the Serbian police from the Ministry of Interior wearing on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: The colour of the uniforms, as I said earlier, is like this colour I have here, but more of a brownish -- the normal police I'm talking about. Because there were four police stations there, and every time I had contact with the police, that was what they were like. It was a mixed colour, a -- it was sort of green, as my jacket is, but more of a brownish in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe that you said earlier that this uniform was different from that worn by the paramilitaries and others. Can you describe the difference that you make between these two types of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I didn't really notice a difference in the uniforms too much. I just knew who were the normal police. I noticed their badges, their belts. I know they had boots more than shoes, whereas the paramilitary didn't have belts. Their jackets were hanging down and they had different arms compared to the normal police. They didn't have any markings on their head gear. That's what they were like.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned head-gear. During your time spent in Pristina, what type of head-gear did the normal police have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: The normal police had caps of the same colour as their clothes, but they didn't have insignia on the caps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say "caps," did this head-gear have bills on the front?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't really understand the last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My question was: When you say "caps," did this head gear have protrusions from the front?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: A type of visor to shade the eyes from the sun, so we are on the same definition, I guess?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they were like.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, in paragraph 15 of your statement you describe an encounter with the police from December of 1998. Now, first of all, did those police have -- or strike that. What type of uniform did those police have? Is it the same that we've talked about here is it different in any way that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: They had the same uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And at that time, and in fact for quite some -- many years prior to that, wasn't it the law of the country you lived in that all citizens had to carry their official ID cards with them at all times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. Every citizen had to have ID with him, but of course people did forget their ID. And on that case I forgot mine at the moment I needed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you produced your ID, those police let you go on your way - isn't that correct - without any repercussions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes, of course. They were normal police, and I showed my documents to them. I thanked them, and they let me go and everything was okay. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, at paragraphs 16 through 18 of your statement you detail, I'll say, another encounter with the individual named Rambo, that you've called Rambo, in early 1999. And I want to ask you: At that time was he wearing the same uniform that you described from the raid in 1996 or 1997, since you said that uniforms changed all the time? Was this the same uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes, the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, was Rambo alone or were other people with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: There were three or four policemen there. They broke into the restaurant a couple of times and there were three or four of them. They -- they raided all the shops.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I want to make sure we're talking about the same incident. I'm not talking about the raids in 1996 and 1997 when you worked for somebody else; I'm talking about the incident you describe at paragraph 16 in January 1999 when this individual named Rambo came to your shop, the shop that you owned and opened. Are we talking about the same event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes, we're talking about the same event. I told you about Rambo, what -- the time he came to the shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And first of all, with respect to Rambo, what type of head-gear was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: He was wearing a police cap, a normal police cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at that time did he have any insignia or other identifying badges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He had a badge.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you describe the location of the badge and the type of badge? What was it made of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: The badge was of metallic, iron maybe, I don't know the exact metal because I'm not an expert in metals.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. For the remainder of my cross-examination, when I refer to a badge, do you understand -- or can we understand each other that I'm talking about a metallic badge? Is that fair enough?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, apart from the badge, did he have a name-tag on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I didn't see any name written, but I imagine there was one. I just didn't see it. I wasn't that close to him to be able to read the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you just mentioned for the first time here today that Rambo came with some other individuals. Could you describe how these people were attired. Did they also have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm trying to do the best to give you an answer. Rambo came into my burek shop, came into the shop, Rambo himself. But what you're talking about is something else, another incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I had asked you about and you said we were talking about the same incident. Let me try and ask a simple question. Do you have your -- a copy of your statement in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes, I have a copy in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just simply want to know with respect to paragraph 16 of that statement, and it's my understanding the paragraphs are the same in the Albanian version. When you discuss the incident at paragraph 16 when Rambo came to your shop, was he alone or were other people with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes, this is right here. 16, but here I'm talking about the burek shop, but there was another incident with Rambo at the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just confine yourself to the burek shop. Was he alone or was he with other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he was alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- now that we're on the same page about the incident, the description you provided of what this guy Rambo was wearing, does that accurately reflect what he was wearing at the time of this particular incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you did not report the incident that is set forth in paragraph 16 with Rambo to anyone in the police station, did you? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you mentioned that there was another incident with Rambo. Would it be safe to say that you had multiple incidents with Rambo during the time period that you had your own shop and prior to that time period when you worked in the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, if the material that has been provided for -- to me by the Office of the Prosecutor is correct, it would seem that your first encounter with this individual, Rambo, occurred sometime in the early 1990s. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Not the year 1990, but sometime in the early 1990s.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes, it was after 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many times you had any run-ins or encounters with Mr. Rambo from 1990 -- from sometime after 1990 through 1999, in total? How many encounters did you have with this individual, Rambo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I encountered him I think only three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it all of these encounters were hostile in nature, were they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Well, I can assure you, if he had come in a friendly manner, he would have come and had a cup of coffee, but it was different. I would say it was hostile.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this was over a span of several years; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you at any point in time seek out or determine what the full name of this individual, Rambo, was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: No, because sometimes they called him Rexhe, sometimes they called him Rambo. He never had the same name. It depends who was with him. Different people called him by different names.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Is Rexhe a Serbian name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Oh, he was -- it's an Albanian name, but that's what they called him. His friends, they would say: Hey, where are you Rexho? Or where are you going, Rambo? Or Rinxho. Things like that. There were always a lot -- other people around him and that -- they called him by different names.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right, sir, now I want to move on to other parts of your statement to try and clear up a few details that are now nagging me. Now, with respect to paragraph 28 of your statement, and if I could ask you to turn to that paragraph just to make sure we're talking about the same event. At that paragraph, you describe something from April of -- April 1st of 1999, when you were on your way back home after receiving a telephone call from your neighbour. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your statement, you identify an event where people were being expelled and say -- and you state that the police were the ones who were doing the expelling. Is that what the statement says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you -- is it correct that you met with and talked with the Office of the Prosecutor on August the 19th, 2006?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you meet with and talk with the Prosecutor of this Tribunal on August the 19th, 2006?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you meet and talk with the Prosecutor -- with the -- with someone from the Prosecutor's office at any time in the past two weeks, prior to giving your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: No, I didn't, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you -- did you meet with the two individuals, the gentleman seated at the end of the bench of the Prosecution's side and the lady seated in the middle of the bench on the Prosecution's side at any point in time prior to giving your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I see them, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, did you tell anyone from the Prosecutor's office that, in fact, relative to paragraph 28 you did not see the regular police during this act of expulsion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I didn't see normal police, regular police, there expelling people.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then -- when in your statement at paragraph 28 where it says, "The police were not there protecting them, they were expelling them," what type of uniforms did the individuals who were doing this act wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I don't know how to describe the uniforms. They were sort of camouflage uniforms, and they had weapons with them. They had black caps or like masks on their faces. That's the type of people they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, earlier I believe you told me that the police that you saw in Pristina had green caps. Is it -- am I correct in reading your testimony to say that the people that were undertaking the acts of expelling people in paragraph 28, that they did -- that they had black caps. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: The normal police had camouflage green uniforms and a cap, whereas the paramilitaries wore masks on their faces and they had long boots and camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say "the paramilitaries," you are not referring to personnel of the Ministry of Interior, are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: The normal police, the MUP, as far as I know, whereas the military who were around, they looked totally different.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you -- perhaps you did not understand my question. Who are you referring to when you call people "paramilitaries"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: What I mean by "paramilitaries" are people who came from outside of Kosova, who were members of organisations to come to Kosova and to do what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So when we use the word "paramilitary," we are not talking about the Serbian police from the Ministry of Interior, are we?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So at paragraph 28, the events that you saw there, were these paramilitaries that did this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I would say 70 per cent were paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What type of uniforms did these individuals have on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: You mean the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: They had black masks and red caps. Secondly, they had green uniforms, but I didn't get close enough to look at them. But from 4 or 5 metres away, when I was leaving, I took a glance at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did they have any emblems, insignia, or badges? And if so, please describe them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: No, they didn't have any badges or insignia. They had red caps and black masks on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And isn't it accurate that with respect to this incident described in paragraph 28, that there were no regular police present during the expulsion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I didn't see any police protecting the population. I didn't notice them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking you, sir, is that: Isn't it a fact that you did not see police taking part in the acts that are described in paragraph 28?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: No, I didn't see regular police there expelling people, but there were normal, regular police out on the street. But the ones who were expelling people were not regular police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I proceed, can I have some assistance from the Office of the Prosecutor. Are they willing to stipulate that the materials they disclosed to me in fact relate to this witness and that he did meet with them and speak with them and discuss this incident and other incidents with them? Because this is happening too often now, Your Honour, where the materials disclosed to us, we can't make heads or tails of it, and it's impossible to proceed in an efficient and productive cross-examination where material that is disclosed to us differs so very much from the facts that are raised in the testimony of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't seem to have been disabled in any way in the conduct of that cross-examination. The only difficulty that arose was because of the way you started off, by approaching it through the statement, when a simple question to the witness about the nature of the personnel involved in that incident would have got you the answer. Probably could have done it in two questions, I think, if you hadn't done it through the statement. So I don't think you ought to blame the Prosecution for that difficulty. However, the separate matter you raise is the -- as a result of approaching it the way you did, it seems plain to me from all I've seen in the court is that there is an issue that needs to be clarified. Now, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And Your Honour is referring to the issue whether we met with this witness or?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, and it may be that it's an issue for re-examination rather than to be dealt with at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That's what I was intending to do, Your Honours, and if it helps Mr. Ivetic at this point I can certainly stipulate to the fact that what is stated in the supplemental information sheet, who met with this witness and when, is correct from our side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you describe the 3rd of April, 1999, when you state that you were expelled from your building, was your wife with you at all times during that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you could clarify for us, what type of personnel did you see engaged in expelling you and your wife from your home on or about 3 April 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I wasn't really paying attention to this personnel. I was paying attention to my wife who was in a tragic situation and she needed my constant attention until we reached the train station. She was almost fainting. She was extremely ill. She was mentally distressed and needed my assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, I believe that you testified earlier today that it was the police that did this, and I'm going to have to ask you again: What type of uniforms, badges, insignia, or emblems did these persons who you label the police wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: From the time we went out, from the time we were expelled from our house, we saw red hats and black masks. Those were the people who expelled us from our houses and said: Get out of your houses and go wherever you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I believe earlier you had described the persons wearing red hats and black masks as paramilitaries. Was it in fact the paramilitaries who expelled you from your home rather than the Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Well, you know, everything in a uniform we call police. People didn't make the distinction between paramilitaries and police there. I would say that it was the paramilitary who expelled us, but on the street outside there were normal policemen and they did nothing to protect us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you say: "Everything in a uniform we call police" and that people don't make distinctions between paramilitaries and the police, are you telling me that you actually cannot testify with any degree of certainty as to what a particular person in a uniform that did expel you from your home, what they were in fact, whether they were paramilitary, police, or even something else? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I am telling you that they had red hats and black masks. Their uniforms were camouflage. They had boots. They were wearing weapons. Those were the people who expelled us from our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I am trying to ask you to clarify your statement where you say at line 4 of page 87, going on to line 5 of page 87: "Well, you know, everything in a uniform we call police. People didn't make the distinction between paramilitaries and police there." Are you telling me that we cannot with any degree of certainty know from your testimony, when you identify someone as being the police, that in fact they are the Serbian police, that is to say employees of the Serbian Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I am telling you that the normal police from the Ministry of the Interior were not the ones who expelled us from our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But bear in mind, Mr. Ivetic, that the witness has said that there were regular Serb police there who did not intervene to protect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That was going to be my next question, Your Honour. I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you stated that your wife with was you at all times. Are you aware of the fact that your wife has executed a sworn statement for the purpose of this Tribunal describing the expulsion and the travel from your home to the train station and has, in that sworn statement, said that she did not see any police that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I don't know about that. That was not my statement. You would have to ask her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ivetic, find a suitable place to interrupt, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, if I ask another question, I was about to move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There's a possibility I might open up a whole new slew of questions. So I think now is the best time and I will take up tomorrow with the remainder of my cross, which hopefully will not be too long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could we get an estimate of how long the cross-examination for this witness will take?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As on other occasions, I invite you to discuss it with one of the Defence counsel, who hopefully will remain an active spokesperson to give you some indication of the position.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, we have to interrupt your evidence at this stage. That's as much as -- as long as we can sit today, and we will resume hearing this tomorrow afternoon at 2.15. So you need to be back here in time to begin giving evidence at 2.15. Meanwhile, it's vital that you do not, I stress do not, discuss any part of your evidence with - and I again stress - any person at all between now and then, and that means do not discuss the evidence you have given or the evidence you are likely to give later in the case tomorrow. Anything else you can talk about, but that subject, the evidence, is off limits. All right? So we'll adjourn now and resume tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 24th day of August, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.
